chapter_theme: Under the heading பிறர் இயல்பைக் குறிப்பால் உணர்தல், seven verses on knowing others by signs: a small part seen stands for the whole, hidden wrong is seen by others' eyes and leaks through the face, the face mirrors intent, and a person's nature is read from their kin, their birth-group and the company they keep.

142.reading: As one ladleful taken from a great pot shows that all the rice in it is cooked, so in anyone what has been seen should be enough to see the rest, for what is seen becomes the ground of knowing.
142.nuance: The verse argues from a sample: one part of a person, like one ladle of rice, stands for the whole. யார்கண்ணும் is said twice, so the rule is pressed on every person without exception.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way what is seen becomes the reason

story.act: no story; the cook's test of one ladle is the instance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a little seen of a person is sufficient ground for judging the whole of them

143.reading: The wicked, thinking the evil they did is hidden as behind a mountain, do not grasp that their evil is plain, for, the poet tells the lord of the shore, eyes are sharper than arrows.
143.nuance: The mountain image (மலைமறைந்தது) is the wrongdoer's own belief; the proverb answers it with others' eyes, which pierce what he thinks is screened. The address to the lord of the shore (சேர்ப்ப!) is a frame and carries no akam situation.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of the wrongdoer who thinks himself unseen

pazhamozhi.applied_to: evil deeds believed hidden are seen by others' eyes

144.reading: As dampness spreads before a flood arrives, those who carry deceit can be known on sight, the poet tells a bright-eyed woman, for even when they hide it the face tells what the heart has gone towards.
144.nuance: The flood image makes the face's sign a forerunner: the wetness comes before the water, as the face shows the intent before the act. The claim is specific to கள்ளம், deceit that is being hidden (ஒளிப்பினும்), not to feeling in general.

pazhamozhi.literal: the face tells just what the heart has spread towards

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the deceitful who try to conceal their purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: deceit can be read in the face even when it is concealed

145.reading: As one sees in a mirror the parts of one's own body that one cannot see by looking, so for those who can read faces the face itself is enough to know another's intention, as the son's understanding shows the father's.
145.nuance: முன்னம், the inward intention, is the old term for what a sign reveals. The proverb's fit is not plain: it may mean that the outward (the son, the face) shows the inward (the father, the mind), as the reading takes it, or that understanding is inherited, which would bear on the observer's skill rather than on the face.

pazhamozhi.literal: the son's understanding is the father's understanding

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the reader of faces

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what cannot be seen directly is known through the thing that reflects it, as the mind through the face

146.reading: It is hard for one person to discern another's mind, the poet tells a sweet-spoken woman, but everyone takes the colours of their own kin, as birds take many colours according to their lands.
146.nuance: The first two lines grant that minds are hard to read; the proverb offers lineage (குலம்) as the way round the difficulty, so character is made to follow birth-group as plumage follows habitat. குலம் here is kin or lineage, a birth-group, and the verse uses it to rank natures.

norm.note: a claim of the period that a person's nature follows the kin-group of birth

pazhamozhi.literal: birds are of many colours according to their lands

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to people of every kin

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a person's hidden nature can be judged by the colour of their kin

147.reading: A keeper's young daughter, though she had come into the hands of a keeper, refused to eat, saying the food was of the pasture, and the poet tells the lord of the misty hill that one's own birth-group comes out strongly however it is hidden.
147.nuance: The episode is obscure: காப்பான் occurs twice and may name a herdsman and a protector or king, and மேய்ப்பாட்டது is a rare form; the words allow that a girl of herding birth, placed in a higher house, betrayed her birth by a habit about food. சாதி in the proverb is a birth-group term, and the verse uses it to say birth cannot be concealed.

norm.note: a claim of the period that the nature of one's birth-group (சாதி) cannot be hidden

pazhamozhi.literal: even if hidden it will not do: one's own birth-group shows out strongly

story.act: a keeper's young daughter, though in a keeper's hands, would not eat food she called of the pasture

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the marks of birth show through any concealment

148.reading: No effort of probing is needed: whether even sages are of good nature is to be known by the company they keep, the poet tells a carp-eyed woman, and no witnesses are needed, for there is no cooked meal the neighbours do not know of.
148.nuance: The test is extended even to முனிவர், the renouncers whose inner state might seem beyond judging. கரியர் are witnesses: the verse sets aside the formal proof of testimony for the evidence of company and common knowledge.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no cooked food that the neighbourhood does not know

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone, sages included, whose nature is in question

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a person's nature is known from their company without inquiry or witnesses

links.note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the only touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 142 says one part seen of a person, like one ladle from the pot, suffices to judge the whole.
links.teaches: Together they turn the Kural's touchstone into a method of sampling: one need not watch all a person's deeds, since a single act examined stands for the whole as one ladle stands for the pot.
links.list_adds: its cooking image and proverb add the claim that a small sample is enough, which the couplet's touchstone does not say.

links.note: Kural 271 says the five elements within laugh at the deceiver's hidden conduct; Pazhamozhi 143 says the wrongdoer who thinks his deed screened by a mountain is pierced by others' eyes, sharper than arrows.
links.teaches: The pair names two witnesses the hider cannot escape, his own body within and other people's eyes without, so concealed wrong is seen from both sides at once.
links.list_adds: it moves the witness from the body's elements to the onlookers and gives the wrongdoer's false belief, the mountain, that the proverb answers.

links.note: Kural 824 warns of deceivers whose faces smile while their hearts are bitter, so the face hides malice; Pazhamozhi 144 says the deceitful are known on sight because the face tells what the heart intends even when they conceal it.
links.teaches: Read together they disagree on whether a deceiver's face can be trusted to betray him: the Kural fears the face that masks, the Pazhamozhi trusts the face to leak, so the reader must ask whether the skill lies in the face or in the one who reads it.
links.list_adds: its flood image claims the sign comes before the deed and cannot be held back, a confidence the couplet denies.

links.note: Kural 706 says the face, like crystal, shows what is strongest in the heart; Pazhamozhi 144 applies this to deceit held under concealment (ஒளிப்பினும்).
links.teaches: The pair extends the Kural's claim from feeling that shows freely to intent that is actively hidden, and holds that concealment does not stop the face's showing.
links.list_adds: it narrows the couplet to கள்ளம் and adds the condition of hiding, with the flood's dampness as the sign that runs ahead.

links.note: Kural 708 says it is enough to stand and look at the face of those who read the inward; Pazhamozhi 145 says for those who know faces the face suffices to know intention, as a mirror shows one's unseen limbs.
links.teaches: The Kural speaks of the petitioner who needs only show his face to a perceptive master, and the Pazhamozhi gives the reason it suffices: the face works as a mirror that makes the unseen inward visible.
links.list_adds: its mirror image supplies the mechanism the couplet assumes, and its proverb frames face and mind as offspring and source.

links.note: Naladiyar 127 asks who can examine another's mind, since minds and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 146 opens with nearly the same words (ஒருவர் ஒருவர்தம் உள்ளத்தைத் தேரும்) and grants the difficulty, but answers that people take the colour of their kin.
links.teaches: The two share the question almost word for word and part on the answer: the Naladiyar leaves the mind unknowable because conduct misleads, while the Pazhamozhi finds an outside mark, lineage, that it trusts more than conduct.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the Naladiyar's closing despair into a method, making kin the visible plumage of a hidden nature.

links.note: Kural 959 says a sprout shows the soil and speech shows the lineage one was born in; Pazhamozhi 146 runs the inference the other way, using lineage to read the hidden mind, as land shows in a bird's colour.
links.teaches: In the Kural lineage is what is inferred from speech, and in the Pazhamozhi lineage is the evidence from which the mind is inferred, so the pair shows kin serving as both sign and signified in this ethics.
links.list_adds: its bird image matches the Kural's soil image but makes kin the key to another's mind rather than the thing to be found.

links.note: Kural 972 holds birth alike for all living beings and distinction to come from the work done; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own birth-group (தஞ்சாதி) shows through any concealment, as in the keeper's daughter.
links.teaches: The pair sets two views of what makes a person's standing side by side: for the Kural deeds make the difference, for this verse birth leaves a mark no change of house can hide.
links.list_adds: its exemplum and proverb make birth an ineradicable trait shown in a habit of eating, where the couplet makes birth equal and conduct the divider.

links.note: Naladiyar 195 calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage from austerity, learning and effort; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own சாதி breaks through concealment.
links.teaches: Within the same group of ethics works the Naladiyar denies that caste has substance while the Pazhamozhi treats it as a nature that betrays itself, so the group holds no single view of birth.
links.list_adds: its story gives birth an observable trait, which is just what the quatrain denies birth has.

links.note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; Pazhamozhi 148 makes company the test by which others, sages included, are known.
links.teaches: The Kural's claim about where understanding lives becomes, in the Pazhamozhi, a rule of evidence: if a person's nature is in their company, then the company is what an observer should read, even of a sage.
links.list_adds: it extends the couplet to the judging of முனிவர் and sets company above witnesses and inquiry as proof.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 146 reads a hidden mind by kin; Pazhamozhi 148 reads it by the company kept, without inquiry or witnesses.
links.teaches: Within one heading the book offers two outward marks of an inner nature, the group one is born into and the group one chooses, and 148 adds that the second applies even to renouncers who have left their kin.

source_issues: 143 line 4: கணையினுந் கூரியவாம் has ந் before க, where கணையினும் would be expected; taken as கணையினும் in the reading.
147 lines 1-2: the episode of காப்பான் மடமகள் and மேய்ப்பாட்டது is obscure in the text as given; the reading is tentative.
